text: A bird's wing pushes air down and back. The air pushes the bird up and forward. On each downstroke, the long flight feathers close together into a solid surface that grips the air. On the upstroke, they twist and open slightly, so the wing slips back up more easily.

Flight needs a lot of power and very little weight. Birds have both. Their chest [[@muscles|muscles]] are huge, sometimes a third of their weight. Their skeletons are light, with many hollow bones. Many of these features, including hollow bones, wishbones and feathers, were already present in their dinosaur ancestors, as you can read in [[@birds-dinosaurs|how birds came from dinosaurs]].

spots: Long, stiff feathers at the wingtip. Each one twists to grip the air on the downstroke.
Flight muscles attach to a big ridge on the breastbone called the keel. They can be a third of a bird's weight.
Bones with air inside, braced by tiny struts, like a bridge. Light but strong.
The tail steers and brakes, like the rudder of a boat.
A springy V-shaped bone that flexes with every wingbeat.

quiz.reveal: The biggest flight muscles sit on the chest, fixed to a ridge on the breastbone called the keel. A smaller chest muscle lifts the wing again, using a tendon that loops over the shoulder like a rope over a pulley.

sec.t:
Many bird bones are hollow, braced inside with tiny struts like the girders of a bridge. Surprisingly, bird bone itself is not lighter than ours. In 2010, a study found it is actually denser. Birds stay light because their bones are thin-walled and many are fused together, so they need fewer of them.

Birds also breathe in a special way. Air sacs, spread through the body and even into some bones, pump fresh air through the [[@lungs-breathe|lungs]] in one direction. This gives flight muscles a steady supply of oxygen. It is one reason birds can fly at heights where people struggle to breathe.

sec.h: Taking off, landing and staying up
sec.t:
Taking off is the hardest part. Small birds leap into the air, and that jump from the legs gives a lot of the starting push. Big birds such as swans and albatrosses need a run-up, pattering across the water into the wind before they lift off. Landing is a careful stall: the bird swings its body upright, spreads its wings and tail like airbrakes and reaches forward with its feet.

Some birds hardly land at all. In 2016, scientists fitted [[@swifts-swallows|common swifts]] with tiny data loggers and found that some stayed in the air for about ten months without stopping. They eat insects on the wing and seem to doze while gliding high up. Frigatebirds, too, can stay over the ocean for weeks, taking short naps in flight.

Geese, cranes and pelicans often fly in a V. Each bird rides on rising air that spins off the wingtip of the bird ahead, which saves energy. In 2014, scientists who fitted ibises with tiny data loggers found the birds even timed their wingbeats to catch that rising air. The birds also take turns at the front, where flying is hardest.

The same basic idea of pushing air down to get [[lift|lift]] keeps a jumbo jet in the sky. Planes do it with fixed wings and engines instead of muscles, as you can read in [[@airplanes-fly|how planes fly]].

text: Coral is an animal, though it does a good impression of the other two. A coral is a colony of thousands of tiny animals called [[polyp|polyps]], most only a few millimetres across. Each polyp is a soft tube with a mouth at the top, ringed by stinging [[tentacle|tentacles]]. Polyps are cousins of [[@jellyfish-old|jellyfish]] and [[@clownfish|sea anemones]].
Each polyp builds a hard cup of limestone underneath itself. When it dies, new polyps grow on top. Over thousands of years, those cups pile up into reefs.
Tiny [[algae|algae]] live inside the polyps. They make food from sunlight by [[@photosynthesis|photosynthesis]] and share it with their host. They also give coral its colours.

st.prompt: What is coral?
st.reveal: An animal! A coral is made of thousands of tiny animals called polyps, cousins of jellyfish. They build stony skeletons, so reefs feel like rock. And tiny algae living inside them make food from sunlight, so they're a bit of everything!
st.nudge: It really does look like one! But it's actually an animal.

sec.t:
Reefs cover less than 1% of the seabed, but about a quarter of all sea [[species|species]] depend on them at some point in their lives. Fish hide in the branches, octopuses lurk in the cracks, and turtles graze nearby.

Parrotfish scrape algae off coral with beak-like teeth, swallowing bits of limestone too. They grind it up and poop it out as fine white sand. Much of the soft sand on [[tropical|tropical]] beaches started out this way.

The biggest reef system of all, the [[@great-barrier-reef|Great Barrier Reef]] off Australia, stretches for about 2,300 km. That is roughly the straight-line distance from Delhi to Kanyakumari.

Reefs grow only in warm, clear, shallow water, where sunlight can reach the algae. In the USA, the biggest reefs lie off the Florida Keys and around [[@hawaii-islands|Hawaii]]. India has four main reef areas: the Gulf of Kutch in Gujarat, the Gulf of Mannar between Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka, [[@lakshadweep|Lakshadweep]], and [[@india-wonder-andaman-reefs|the Andaman and Nicobar Islands]]. Most reef-building corals grow slowly, often just a centimetre or so a year. Your [[@nails|fingernails]] grow faster.

In 1836, a young Charles Darwin sailed past coral islands in the Indian Ocean and wondered how they formed. He guessed that reefs grow around volcanic islands. As the volcano slowly sinks, the coral keeps building upward, until only a ring of reef is left. This ring is called an [[atoll|atoll]].

More than a hundred years later, drills sank deep into an atoll in the Pacific and hit volcanic rock far below the coral, just as Darwin had predicted.

India's Lakshadweep islands are atolls like these. So the ground under the houses, coconut palms and beaches there was built by polyps.

{{story:climate-change}}

sec.h: When the sea gets too hot
sec.t:
Corals are fussy about temperature. If the water stays even a degree or two warmer than usual for weeks, the polyps push out their algae. Without them, the coral turns ghostly white. This is called bleaching.

A bleached coral is not dead yet. If the water cools soon, the algae can return. If the heat lasts, the coral starves. Long heatwaves in the sea have caused bleaching across the Great Barrier Reef, the Florida Keys and the Lakshadweep and Andaman reefs. In 2024, scientists announced that a worldwide bleaching event was under way, only the fourth ever recorded.

On a few nights each year, many corals on the same reef release eggs and sperm at the same time, often a few days after a full moon. The water fills with drifting pink and white specks, like an upside-down snowstorm.

Divers come from around the world to see it. Scientists are now collecting those eggs, growing baby corals in tanks and planting them back on damaged reefs. Off India's coasts, from the [[@andaman|Andaman Islands]] to the Gulf of Mannar, researchers are testing ways to help reefs recover.

text: At the start of the 1900s, the greater one-horned rhino was in deep trouble. Hunters shot rhinos for sport and for their horns, and farms were swallowing the grasslands where they lived. In Kaziranga, on the banks of the Brahmaputra in Assam, perhaps only a few dozen were left.

In 1905, the British government of the time set Kaziranga aside as a protected forest. Over the next century it became a [[sanctuary|sanctuary]], then a national park in 1974. Forest guards fought off poachers, and the rhinos had space and safety to breed.
The count in 2022 found about 2,600 rhinos in Kaziranga. That is around two-thirds of all the one-horned rhinos on Earth.

st.prompt: What is a rhino's horn made of?
st.reveal: A rhino horn is a solid block of keratin, the same material as hair, nails and hooves. It grows from the skin, not the skull, and if it breaks off it slowly grows back. It has no proven power as a medicine.

sec.t:
There is a famous story about how Kaziranga was saved. In 1904, Mary Curzon, the wife of Lord Curzon, the British Viceroy of India, visited the area hoping to see a rhino. She saw only their footprints, and was so worried that she persuaded her husband to protect the land.

Nobody is sure how much of the story is true, but the dates fit. Kaziranga was declared a proposed reserve forest in 1905. It became a reserve forest in 1908 and a game sanctuary in 1916. In 1950 the word "game" was dropped, because the animals were there to be protected, not shot.

sec.h: Armour, mud and a single horn
sec.t:
A one-horned rhino can weigh over 2 tonnes, about as much as two small cars. Its thick skin hangs in deep folds that make it look as if it is wearing armour plates.

Rhinos spend hot afternoons wallowing in mud and pools, which keeps them cool and protects their skin from insects. They graze on the tall elephant grass that covers much of the park, and they leave large shared dung piles that other rhinos sniff to learn who has passed by.

Strangely, rhinos don't fight with their horns. They slash with sharp lower teeth instead. The horn is mostly for show.

{{story:floods-why}}

Every [[monsoon|monsoon]], the Brahmaputra spills over its banks and floods most of Kaziranga. The floods are good for the grasslands, washing in fresh soil and clearing old growth. But they are hard on the animals.

When the water rises, rhinos, deer and elephants head south across a busy highway to the Karbi Anglong hills. Speed limits and wildlife crossings help them get there. Inside the park, forest staff have built raised mounds of earth where animals can stand above the water.

Rhino horn is worth a great deal of money on illegal markets, mainly because some people believe it is a medicine. It isn't. Poachers have killed hundreds of Kaziranga's rhinos over the years.

Kaziranga answered with hundreds of armed forest guards and anti-poaching camps spread across the park. The approach has saved many rhinos, though some human rights groups have criticised how tough it can be on suspected poachers. In September 2021, Assam publicly burned about 2,500 rhino horns from its stores, to show that horns have no value except on a living rhino.

Kaziranga is also home to tigers, Asian [[@elephants-talk|elephants]], wild water buffalo and swamp deer. It became a UNESCO [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage]] Site in 1985, one of India's best-known [[@national-parks|national parks]].

Rhinos from Kaziranga have also been moved to restart populations elsewhere, such as Manas National Park, which had lost all its rhinos. Together with [[@nepal|Nepal]]'s parks, they have brought the one-horned rhino from the edge of extinction to about 4,000 animals. It is still listed as vulnerable, but it is one of Asia's great wildlife comebacks.

text: To keep time, a clock needs something that repeats at a steady beat, like a heart. That might be the Sun crossing the sky, [[@how-swings|a swinging pendulum]], a buzzing crystal or the tiny [[vibration|vibrations]] of an [[atom|atom]]. Each beat must take exactly the same time as the last.

The second thing a clock needs is a counter. Gears, a [[@chips-silicon|computer chip]] or a person keep track of how many beats have gone by and turn them into seconds, minutes and hours on a dial or screen. The steadier the beat, the better the clock. A good [[pendulum|pendulum]] clock might drift a few seconds a week. The best atomic clocks would take millions of years to drift by one second.

st.reveal: A pendulum's swing time depends mostly on its length. A shorter string swings faster and a longer one swings slower. Weight and how hard you push make almost no difference, which is exactly why pendulums make good clocks.

sec.t:
The oldest clocks used the Sun. A sundial has a pointer that casts a shadow, and the shadow moves around the dial as the Sun crosses the sky. In the 1720s and 1730s, in [[@jaipur|Jaipur]], Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II built the [[@jantar-mantar|Jantar Mantar]], a set of giant stone instruments. Its largest sundial, the Samrat Yantra, is about 27 metres tall. Its shadow moves fast enough for you to watch it creep across the stone.

Sundials don't work at night or on cloudy days. So people in [[@ancient-egypt|ancient Egypt]], [[@babylon|Babylon]], China and India also used water clocks. Water dripped steadily out of one bowl, or into another, and marks showed how much time had passed.

Around 1600, [[@galileo|Galileo]] noticed that a pendulum of a given length takes the same time for every swing, whether the swing is big or small. In 1656, the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens used this to build the first pendulum clock. It was far more accurate than anything before it.

Inside a pendulum clock, a part called the escapement lets the gears turn one tooth at a time with each swing. It also gives the pendulum a tiny push to keep it going. That steady tick-tock sound is the escapement at work. Grandfather clocks in old homes in Kolkata or Boston still run on the same idea.

The most accurate clocks use atoms. Atoms of the metal caesium absorb a particular kind of radio wave at an extremely precise [[frequency|frequency]]. Since 1967, one second has been officially defined as 9,192,631,770 of these vibrations.

Atomic clocks do far more than tell you when school starts. [[@gps-how|GPS]] satellites carry them, and your phone works out where you are by comparing their time signals. An error of just a millionth of a second could put you hundreds of metres off on a map. India's own [[@navic|NavIC satellites]] also carry atomic clocks, and the National Physical Laboratory in New Delhi keeps the country's official time.

text: Light bends when it passes from air into [[@glass-made|glass]] or plastic and out again. This bending is called [[refraction|refraction]]. A lens is a piece of glass or plastic shaped so that it bends light in a planned way.

Your eye already has a lens of its own, just behind the coloured iris. Together with the clear front of the eye, it focuses light into a sharp picture on the [[retina|retina]], the light-sensitive layer at the back. If your eyeball is a little too long or too short, or the lens can't change shape enough, the picture lands slightly in the wrong place and looks blurry. Glasses add one more lens in front of your eye, nudging the light so the picture lands exactly on the retina again.

myth: Wearing glasses makes your eyes weaker, so you'll need them more and more.

Glasses don't weaken eyes. Short sight in children often gets stronger as they grow, with or without glasses, which is why the prescription changes. Not wearing glasses you need just makes things blurry and can give you headaches.

sec.t:
If you can read a book easily but the board at school is fuzzy, you are short-sighted. Light from far away comes into focus just in front of the retina. Glasses for short sight are thinner in the middle than at the edges. These *concave* lenses spread light out a little.

If faraway things are clear but close-up reading is hard, you may be long-sighted. Then the focus falls behind the retina. *Convex* lenses, thicker in the middle, gather the light in sooner. A [[@magnifying-glass|magnifying glass]] is a strong convex lens.

As people reach their forties, the lens inside the eye stiffens and can't change shape as easily. That's why many grandparents hold a phone at arm's length, or wear reading glasses.

Put two lenses together in the right way, and you can see things nobody had seen before. Around 1610, [[@galileo|Galileo]] turned a [[@telescopes-how|telescope]] towards the night sky and spotted moons circling Jupiter. In the 1670s, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Dutch cloth merchant, built tiny single-lens [[@microscopes|microscopes]] and saw [[bacteria|bacteria]] swimming in drops of water.

[[@cameras-how|Cameras]], [[@made-phone-screens|phone screens]], [[@projectors|projectors]] and car headlights all use lenses. So do your eyes, every second they are open.

Short sight has become much more common, especially in East Asia, where in some cities most young adults are short-sighted. It is rising in India and the USA too. One major study estimated that about half the world's people could be short-sighted by 2050.

Scientists think the change is partly about how children spend their days. Time outdoors in bright daylight seems to help protect against short sight, while long hours of close-up work, including [[@screen-time|screens]], may add to the risk. If the board looks blurry, tell a parent or teacher. A quick eye test, which is painless, can sort it out, and the glasses that follow can make a school day much easier.

text: If Earth's [[gravity|gravity]] doubled, everything would weigh twice as much. You would feel as if you were carrying another person on your back all day. Jumping, climbing stairs and even lifting your arms would be hard work.

Things would fall faster, so trips and spills would hurt more. The air would be pressed down harder too, roughly doubling the pressure at ground level. Rockets would struggle to reach space. Over time, plants and animals would probably [[evolve|evolve]] to be shorter, stockier and stronger. This can't really happen to Earth, but it's a great way to see how much gravity shapes our lives.

st.reveal: Your legs would have to lift twice the weight with the same muscles, and gravity would also pull you back twice as hard. Together that cuts your jump to well under half its usual height.

sec.t:
Your heart would have to pump harder to push blood up to your brain. Fighter pilots feel several times their normal weight in tight turns, and without special suits, blood drains from their heads and they can black out. Double gravity is gentler than that, but it would never let up.

Your bones and muscles would be under constant strain. Knees and backs would ache. Astronauts in space lose bone because gravity is too weak. Here, the problem would flip. Bones would likely grow thicker over a lifetime, as they do in people who carry heavy loads.

And your jump? It would be far less than half its usual height, because your legs would have to lift twice the weight, and gravity would drag you back twice as hard.

sec.h: A world in a pressure cooker
sec.t:
The air presses down on us because gravity pulls it towards the ground. Double gravity would roughly double that push.

That would change cooking. Water boils at 100°C at normal pressure. At double pressure, it boils at about 120°C. That's exactly what a [[@pressure-cooker|pressure cooker]] does in an Indian kitchen to cook rice and dal faster. With double gravity, every open pot would act a bit like one.

Denser air would also push harder against anything moving through it, from cricket balls to birds.

Tall trees, like the [[@redwoods|redwoods]] of California, must lift water more than 100 metres up their trunks. Stronger gravity would make that much harder. Forests would probably be shorter.

Animals would feel it too. When an animal doubles in size, its weight grows much faster than the strength of its legs. That's why elephants have thick, pillar-like legs while spiders can have thin ones. With double gravity, the biggest animals, like elephants and giraffes, would struggle most. Over millions of years, life would likely become lower and sturdier.

To leave Earth, a rocket must reach about 11.2 km every second. If Earth had twice the mass at the same size, that would rise to about 16 km a second. Rockets would need far more fuel, and big rockets might barely get off the ground.

A German scientist calculated in 2018 that on some heavy "super-Earth" planets, chemical rockets might hardly be able to reach space at all. If aliens live on such worlds, they may be stuck at home.

You can't double Earth's gravity, but you can borrow the feeling. A [[@how-roller-coaster-loop|roller coaster]] pulling out of a dip, or a lift starting upward, briefly makes you feel heavier.

On the giant planets, the pull is real. At the cloud tops of Jupiter, gravity is about 2.5 times stronger than on Earth, so a 30 kg child would weigh as much as a 75 kg adult. Every world has its own pull, which is why your weight changes so much across [[@gravity-planets|the planets]]. Even a [[@sky-skydiving|skydiver]] would plunge noticeably faster under Jupiter-like gravity.

text: When water freezes, its molecules hold hands in a roomy six-sided pattern.

In liquid water, each [[molecule|molecule]] jostles about, packing in quite close to its neighbours. As water freezes, the molecules lock into a neat, open framework with gaps in the middle, like a honeycomb. The same amount of water now takes up about 9% more space. So ice has a lower [[density|density]] than liquid water, and it floats.
Because ice floats, lakes freeze from the top down. The ice acts like a lid, and fish survive in the water below.
If ice sank, many lakes would freeze solid from the bottom up.

st.reveal: Water expands when it freezes, by about 9%. Its molecules lock into an open, hexagon-shaped pattern with gaps. So ice is lighter than the same amount of liquid water, and floats.
st.nudge: Some ice does have bubbles! But even perfectly clear ice floats.

myth: Icebergs are frozen seawater.

Icebergs are chunks broken off glaciers and ice sheets, which formed from snow that fell on land, so they are made of fresh water. Frozen seawater is a different thing, called sea ice, and it's usually much thinner.

sec.t:
Each water molecule is made of one oxygen [[atom|atom]] and two hydrogen atoms. The hydrogen ends are slightly positive and the oxygen end slightly negative, so molecules cling to each other with weak links called hydrogen bonds.

In liquid water, these links keep breaking and re-forming as the molecules tumble around. In ice, they hold firm, and each molecule links to four neighbours at fixed angles. That arrangement builds the six-sided pattern you can see in [[@snowflake-six|snowflakes]].

Most liquids get steadily heavier as they cool. Water does too, until about 4°C. Below that, it starts to expand again, as molecules begin lining up into their icy pattern.

That matters for lakes. In winter, water at 4°C sinks to the bottom, and colder water floats on top until it freezes. A frozen lake can have ice on top and water at about 4°C below, where fish, frogs and plants wait out the winter.

Only a few other substances, such as silicon and the metals gallium and bismuth, also expand when they freeze. Drop a cube of solid butter or wax into its own melted liquid, and it sinks, the way most solids do.

{{story:titanic}}

An iceberg floats with about 90% of its bulk hidden under the sea. Only the top tenth shows, which is where the saying "the tip of the iceberg" comes from.

In April 1912, the [[@titanic|Titanic]] struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic. The crew had seen only the part above water. Icebergs are pieces of [[@glaciers|glaciers]] and [[@what-if-ice-melted|ice sheets]] that break off where they meet the sea, mostly from Greenland and Antarctica. They're made of fresh water from snow that fell long ago.

Because water expands as it freezes, it can push with great force. A sealed glass bottle of water left in a freezer may crack. Pipes can burst in cold winters, which is why people in very [[@cold-places|cold places]] let taps drip or wrap their pipes.

In mountains, rainwater seeps into cracks in rock, freezes at night and widens the cracks. Over many years, this breaks boulders apart. It's one of the ways the Himalaya is slowly worn down, sending rock and soil into the [[@rivers-himalaya|rivers]] below.

In winter, the high-altitude lake [[@india-wonder-pangong|Pangong Tso]] in [[@ladakh|Ladakh]] freezes over, even though its water is salty. Temperatures there can fall far below freezing. Further north, in places like Canada and the northern USA, lakes freeze thick enough for people to fish through holes in the ice and play ice hockey on top.

On [[@moons-of-jupiter|Jupiter's moon]] [[@europa|Europa]], scientists think a thick shell of ice may float on [[@space-weird-oceans-moons|a hidden ocean]] in the same way. Under every one of those frozen surfaces, life carries on in the darker water below, protected by a lid of floating ice.

sec.h: फ़ेरमेयर की नकल करने वाला आदमी
sec.t:
योहानेस फ़ेरमेयर 1600 के दशक के एक डच चित्रकार थे, जो खिड़की से आती रोशनी वाले शांत दृश्यों के लिए मशहूर हैं। उनकी बस लगभग 35 पेंटिंगें ज्ञात हैं, इसलिए कोई "नई" मिल जाए तो वह बेशकीमती होगी। 1930 के दशक में हान फ़ान मेगेरेन नाम के एक डच कलाकार ने नई-नई "फ़ेरमेयर" बनानी शुरू कीं। उसने ऐसे धार्मिक विषय चुने, जिनके बारे में कुछ जानकारों को उम्मीद थी कि फ़ेरमेयर ने कभी बनाए होंगे। वह पुराने कैनवस इस्तेमाल करता और तस्वीरों को ओवन में पकाता था। रंग में एक तरह का प्लास्टिक मिलाता, ताकि रंग पुराने रंग की तरह सख़्त होकर चटक जाए। बड़े-बड़े जानकार धोखा खा गए।

[[@world-war-two|दूसरे विश्व युद्ध]] के बाद डच अफ़सरों को उसकी एक "फ़ेरमेयर" नाज़ी नेता हरमन गोरिंग के संग्रह में मिली। देश का खज़ाना दुश्मन को बेचने के आरोप में फ़ान मेगेरेन गिरफ़्तार हुआ। खुद को बचाने के लिए उसने कबूल किया कि वह नकली थी, और अफ़सरों की आँखों के सामने एक और "फ़ेरमेयर" बना डाली। 1947 में अदालत ने [[verdict|फ़ैसला]] सुनाया कि वह जालसाज़ी का दोषी है, और कुछ ही हफ़्तों बाद उसकी मौत हो गई।

असली पेंटिंग आम तौर पर अपने पीछे एक पगडंडी छोड़ती है: चिट्ठियाँ, बिक्री की रसीदें, प्रदर्शनियों की सूचियाँ, पुरानी तस्वीरें और फ़्रेम के पीछे चिपके लेबल। जालसाज़ यह जानते हैं, इसलिए सबसे चालाक जालसाज़ यह पगडंडी भी नकली बना लेते हैं।

जर्मन जालसाज़ वोल्फ़गांग बेल्ट्राकी 20वीं सदी की शुरुआत के मशहूर कलाकारों के अंदाज़ में "नई" पेंटिंगें गढ़ता, फिर दावा करता कि वे किसी मशहूर पुराने संग्रह से आई हैं। उसने नकली पुरानी तस्वीरें तक बनाईं, जिनमें उसकी पत्नी अपनी ही नानी का भेस धरकर पेंटिंगों के पास बैठी थी। 2010 में उसकी कहानी बिखर गई। वैज्ञानिकों ने 1914 की तारीख वाली एक पेंटिंग जाँची और उसमें टाइटेनियम व्हाइट पाया, एक ऐसा रंग जो उसके कई साल बाद तक कलाकारों को बिकता ही नहीं था।

प्रयोगशालाएँ किसी पेंटिंग की सामग्री की उम्र जाँच सकती हैं। नमक के दाने से भी छोटा रंग का एक कण बता देता है कि कौन से [[pigment|रंगद्रव्य]] इस्तेमाल हुए। [[@x-rays|एक्स-रे]] छिपी परतें दिखाते हैं और यह भी कि कहीं किसी पुराने कैनवस को खुरचकर दोबारा तो इस्तेमाल नहीं किया गया। लकड़ी और कैनवस की उम्र कार्बन से निकाली जा सकती है, उसी [[@half-life|अर्ध-आयु]] वाले तरीके से जिससे प्राचीन हड्डियों की उम्र आँकी जाती है।

विज्ञान यह साबित करने में माहिर है कि कोई पेंटिंग ज़रूरत से ज़्यादा नई है। पर यह साबित करना कि पेंटिंग असली है, कहीं कठिन है, क्योंकि पुराने रंग वाला पुराना कैनवस भी बहुत पहले के किसी माहिर नकलची का काम हो सकता है। इसके लिए जानकारों को सारे सुराग एक साथ तौलने पड़ते हैं।

कुछ सवालों के जवाब अब भी खुले हैं। ईसा मसीह की पेंटिंग *साल्वातोर मुंडी* 2017 में [[@leonardo|लियोनार्दो दा विंची]] की कृति के रूप में लगभग 45 करोड़ अमेरिकी डॉलर में नीलाम हुई। नीलामी में आज तक कोई पेंटिंग इससे महँगी नहीं बिकी। कुछ जानकारों को अब भी शक है कि इसका ज़्यादातर हिस्सा लियोनार्दो ने बनाया था।

text: The Constitution says how India is governed, what the government can and can't do, and what rights every person has. Every law in India must fit inside it. If a law breaks it, courts can cancel that law.

It promises things like equality before the law, [[@free-speech|freedom of speech]], and free education for children. It also sets up [[@parliament-india|Parliament]], the courts, the President and the [[@election-commission|Election Commission]], and explains how they work together.

The original was written by hand by Prem Behari Narain Raizada, a master of [[@calligraphy|calligraphy]]. It was decorated by the artist [[@nandalal-bose|Nandalal Bose]] and his students, who had studied the Ajanta paintings.

For nearly three years they debate every word. Dr B.R. Ambedkar leads the drafting committee.

sec.h: Writing a rulebook for a new nation
sec.t:
In December 1946, the [[@constituent-assembly|Constituent Assembly]] met in New Delhi to write the Constitution. After [[@partition|Partition]], it had 299 members, including 15 women, such as [[@sarojini-naidu|Sarojini Naidu]], Hansa Mehta and Ammu Swaminathan.

Dr B.R. [[@ambedkar|Ambedkar]] chaired the drafting committee. Members studied the constitutions of many countries, including the USA, Britain, Ireland and Canada. They argued over almost every line for nearly three years. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949, now Constitution Day, and came into force on 26 January 1950, now Republic Day.

Every person gets rights like equality before the law and freedom of speech. Untouchability, the old practice of treating some castes as "unclean", was abolished. Children aged 6–14 have the right to free education, added in 2002.

In 1976, a list of Fundamental Duties was added too. It asks citizens to respect the flag and anthem, protect the environment and develop a scientific temper, which means thinking with evidence.

The Constitution can be amended, which means changed by Parliament following special rules. It has been amended more than 100 times.

But there are limits. In 1973, the [[@supreme-courts|Supreme Court]] ruled that Parliament cannot change the Constitution's "basic structure", such as [[democracy|democracy]] and the rule of law.

sec.h: How it works in daily life
sec.t:
The Constitution can feel far away, but it touches ordinary days. It is the reason elections are held every five years, and why every adult citizen gets one vote, whatever their caste, religion or wealth. It sets up free and fair voting through the Election Commission.

It divides work between the central government and the states. Defence and railways belong to the centre, while police and public health belong mainly to the states. Education is shared. When you go to a government school, ride a train or see a police officer, you are seeing the Constitution at work.

The two handwritten originals, one in Hindi and one in English, are kept in special cases filled with helium gas in the Library of Parliament, to stop them decaying. On 24 January 1950, members of the Assembly signed them one by one. Today, you can read the whole Constitution free online, in many Indian languages.

text: People move to new countries for many reasons. Most go for work, hoping for better pay or a job that matches their skills. Others go to study, to join family who moved earlier, or to marry. Some have no choice: they flee war, [[persecution|persecution]] or disaster.

Experts talk about "push" and "pull" factors. Push factors drive people away from home, like poverty, conflict or a failed harvest. Pull factors draw them somewhere new, like jobs, safety, good universities or relatives already there. In 2020, about 28 crore people, roughly 1 in every 28 people on Earth, were living outside the country where they were born.

st.reveal: Most migrants move for work, study or to join family. In 2020 there were about 2.6 crore refugees among about 28 crore international migrants. Refugees face the hardest journeys, but they are a minority of people on the move.

sec.t:
India has the largest group of people living abroad of any country, about 1.8 crore. Many work in the Gulf countries, such as the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, building, nursing and running businesses. Others live in the USA, the UK, [[@canada|Canada]] and Australia. Indian workers abroad send home more than 100 billion dollars a year, more money than is sent to any other country. Families use it for houses, school fees and medical bills.

Some Indians who went to study abroad became famous there. [[@kalpana-chawla|Kalpana Chawla]] moved from Karnal, Haryana, to study in the United States, and later became the first woman of Indian origin to fly in space.

The United States is often called a nation of [[@ellis-island|immigrants]]. Between 1892 and 1954, more than 12 million people arrived through Ellis Island in New York harbour, many from Italy, Ireland, Germany and Eastern Europe. As their ships came in, they passed the [[@statue-liberty|Statue of Liberty]]. A poem by Emma Lazarus on its base speaks of welcoming "huddled masses yearning to breathe free".

Today the US has more immigrants than any other country, around 5 crore. [[@new-york|New York]] is home to people speaking hundreds of languages.

Migrants often bring their food, music and festivals with them, and these change their new homes. Chicken tikka masala is a favourite dish in Britain, and [[@diwali-lights|Diwali]] is celebrated in New York's [[@times-square|Times Square]]. In Trinidad, people of Indian descent play chutney music that mixes Bhojpuri songs with Caribbean [[rhythm|rhythms]].

Moving is rarely easy. Migrants may leave behind parents, friends and familiar food, and face a new language, a new [[climate|climate]] and sometimes unkind treatment. Countries argue about how many newcomers to let in and on what terms, and opinions differ widely, in India and the USA alike.

Most migration does not cross borders at all. Far more people move within their own country, especially from villages to [[@cities-grow|growing cities]]. Almost every family's story, if you go back far enough, includes someone who packed a bag and left home for somewhere new.

text: A Möbius strip is a loop with a half-twist. You make one by taking a strip of paper, flipping one end over and joining it to the other.

That small twist changes everything. A normal loop, like a bangle or a rubber band, has two sides, inside and outside, and two edges. A Möbius strip has just one side and one edge. Run your finger along its surface and you will travel over what looked like both the "front" and "back" before arriving where you started. It is pronounced "MUR-bee-us" or "MOE-bee-us".

st.reveal: Most people guess two loops, but the strip opens into one long loop with two full twists in it. That new loop has two sides. Try it and you will probably want to do it again.

myth: A Möbius strip is just a twisted ring with two sides, like any loop.
An ordinary loop has an inside and an outside. A Möbius strip has only one surface. An ant could walk over every part of it and return to its starting point without ever crossing an edge.

sec.t:
In 1858, two German mathematicians found this shape at about the same time, without knowing of each other. Johann Listing seems to have found it a few weeks earlier. But August Möbius described it more fully, and his work became better known, so the strip carries his name.

They were studying a new kind of maths called topology. It asks what stays the same about a shape when you bend, stretch or squash it, as long as you don't cut or glue it. To a topologist, a coffee mug and a doughnut count as the same shape, because each has exactly one hole.

Cut a Möbius strip down the middle and you might expect two loops. Instead, you get one loop, twice as long, with two full twists. It now has two sides.

Cut a strip one-third of the way in from the edge, and something even stranger happens. You get two loops linked together like chain links. One is a new, thinner Möbius strip. The other is a longer two-sided loop. Many maths teachers love this trick because almost nobody predicts it.

You can keep going. Give a strip a full twist instead of a half, then cut it down the middle. This time you really do get two loops, but they come out linked together. Three half-twists and a cut give you a single loop tied in a knot.

Long ago, some factories used belts to carry power from an engine to machines. A plain belt wears out on one side only. A belt with a half-twist wears evenly on its one surface, so it can last twice as long. The same idea has been used for conveyor belts and old typewriter ribbons.

In 1970, a college student in the USA named Gary Anderson won a design contest with a symbol of three arrows folded into a loop. It is a Möbius strip, and it became the worldwide symbol for [[@recycling|recycling]].

Artists and builders keep returning to this shape. There are Möbius roller coasters, Möbius [[sculpture|sculptures]] and even buildings shaped like the strip. Chemists have made [[molecule|molecules]] joined in a Möbius loop.

Some mathematicians enjoy an even weirder cousin, the Klein bottle. It is a bottle whose inside and outside are the same surface, though a true one can't be built in our three-dimensional world. Shapes that look possible but cannot exist have their own story in [[@puzzle-impossible-shapes|impossible shapes]].

text: A [[@logic|logic]] puzzle gives you a few facts and asks you to work out something that follows from them. You don't need special knowledge, just careful thinking.

Most logic puzzles rely on two tools. **Deduction** means reasoning from what you know: if all cats have tails, and Kitty is a cat, Kitty has a tail. **Elimination** means crossing out possibilities that can't be true, until only one is left. Detectives in stories work this way, and so do people solving [[@sudoku|Sudoku]].
Good puzzles feel impossible at first, then obvious once you see the trick.

st.prompt: On an island, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. You meet someone who says: "I am a knave." What is going on?

options.t: Nobody on the island could say that

st.reveal: A knight can't say it, because it would be a lie. A knave can't say it either, because it would be true. So nobody on the island could ever say "I am a knave". Puzzles like this train you to test each possibility in turn.

sec.h: A puzzle older than most castles
sec.t:
One of the oldest puzzle collections in Europe is linked to Alcuin of York. He was an English scholar who taught at the court of the emperor Charlemagne around 800 CE. It was made to sharpen the minds of young students.

It contains the river-crossing puzzle. A farmer has a wolf, a goat and a cabbage, and a boat that carries only him and one of them. Left alone, the wolf will eat the goat, and the goat will eat the cabbage. How does he get them all across?

The trick is that the farmer may take something back the way he came. He takes the goat over first, then comes back for the wolf, but brings the goat back with him. Leaving the goat, he takes the cabbage across, and finally returns for the goat.

In 1883, the French mathematician Édouard Lucas [[@puzzle-tower-hanoi|sold a puzzle with three pegs]] and a stack of discs of different sizes. You must move the stack to another peg, one disc at a time, never putting a bigger disc on a smaller one.

Three discs take at least 7 moves. Four take 15. Each extra disc doubles the moves and adds one. Lucas sold the puzzle with a story about temple priests moving 64 golden discs, with the world ending when they finished. That would take 2⁶⁴ − 1 moves, more than 18 billion billion. At one move per second, that's about 585 billion years, far longer than the universe has existed.

Computer science students still study the puzzle, because its neat step-by-step solution is a good example of an [[@algorithms|algorithm]].

Many magazine logic puzzles give you a set of clues about people, pets and houses, and a grid to fill in. "The person with the dog lives next to the red house." You tick what's true and cross out what can't be.

The most famous is the "zebra puzzle", which asks who owns the zebra. It is often said to have been written by [[@einstein|Einstein]]. It actually first appeared in a magazine called *Life International* in 1962, seven years after he died.

Logic puzzles train the same thinking used in maths proofs, computer programs and [[@chess-india|chess]]. Programmers use logical rules to make computers check every possibility. Scientists use elimination to rule out wrong explanations. And sometimes people just like the click of an answer falling into place.

text: Numbers themselves can't lie. A count is a count. But people choose which numbers to show, how to show them and what to leave out. That can make true numbers tell a false story.

Some tricks are on purpose, used by advertisers or people trying to win an argument. Many more are honest mistakes. The good news is that most of them fall into a few patterns, and once you know them, you start spotting them everywhere.

In 1954, an American writer named Darrell Huff wrote a short, funny book called *How to Lie with Statistics*. It was meant as a warning, not a guide, and it became one of the best-selling [[statistics|statistics]] books ever written.

st.prompt: In summer, more ice cream is sold, and more people get sunburnt. What's the best explanation?

options.t: Sunburn makes people want ice cream

st.reveal: Two things rising together doesn't mean one causes the other. Here a third thing, sunny weather, is behind both. Scientists call this a hidden cause, and it trips people up all the time.

sec.t:
During the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], American military planners studied bombers coming back from missions. The planes were peppered with bullet holes on the wings and body, but had far fewer near the engines. The obvious plan was to add armour where the holes were.

A mathematician named Abraham Wald, working with a team of statisticians in New York, saw the problem. The planners were only looking at planes that had come back. Planes hit in the engines mostly never returned. The places with no holes were the most dangerous places to be hit.

This mistake is called survivorship bias. It happens whenever you only look at the winners. If you only study famous people who dropped out of college, you might think dropping out leads to success, because you never hear about the many who struggled.

sec.h: Together is not the same as because

sec.t:
Suppose a headline says eating a certain snack "doubles your risk" of an illness. That sounds scary. But if the risk goes from 1 in 10,000 people to 2 in 10,000, the change is tiny for any one person.

[[percentage|Percentages]] can do this in both directions. A rise "from 1 to 2" is a 100% rise. A rise from 50 to 60 is only 20%. Always ask: [[@percentages|per cent]] of what?

Small groups cause trouble too. If an advert says "4 out of 5 people preferred our toothpaste", you'd want to know whether that meant 5 people or 5,000.

The quickest way to change a story is to change the [[@graphs-charts|chart]]. If a bar chart's [[axis|axis]] starts at 95 instead of 0, a score of 96 can look twice as tall as 95. A line graph that is stretched tall makes a gentle rise look like a cliff.

Averages can mislead as well. A company might say its "average" salary is high, using the mean, when a few big bosses earn most of the money. The [[@averages|median]] tells a truer story.

The American writer [[@mark-twain|Mark Twain]] popularised the saying "There are three kinds of lies: lies, damned lies and statistics." He credited it to Benjamin Disraeli, a British prime minister. Researchers have searched Disraeli's writings and speeches and never found it there, so its true origin is unknown.

Statistics are still one of the best tools we have for understanding the world, from [[@vaccines|vaccines]] to [[@news-media|news reports]]. The trick is to ask good questions before believing the answer.

text: Serena Williams is an American [[@tennis|tennis]] player, and many people consider her the greatest woman ever to play the game. She won 23 [[@tennis-grand-slams|Grand Slam]] singles titles, the most by any player since professionals were allowed into the big [[tournament|tournaments]] in 1968. She also won four Olympic gold medals and 14 Grand Slam doubles titles with her sister Venus.
She played professionally for about 27 years. Her powerful serve and fierce style changed women's tennis, and she became one of the most famous athletes on the planet.

Her serve was one of the best ever, but she also won with clever shot choices, fast movement and great returns. Many experts call her the best competitor tennis has seen when a match was close.

sec.t:
Serena was born in Saginaw, Michigan, in 1981, the youngest of five sisters. The family moved to Compton, in [[@los-angeles|Los Angeles]] county. Her father, Richard Williams, had decided to make two of his daughters tennis champions, and wrote a long plan for their careers before they were even born, according to his own account.

He taught Venus and Serena on public courts, often worn and cracked. The girls practised for hours. When they were about ten and nine, the family moved to Florida for better coaching.

Serena's serve was her most famous weapon. It was fast, accurate and hard to read, because she used almost the same toss for different serves. She hit hard from the back of the court and moved well for a powerful player.

She also fought back from losing positions again and again. In tight moments she seemed to raise her level, something players call being clutch. Her [[@muscles|muscles]] were strong, but her planning and nerve were just as important.

She was ranked world number one for 319 weeks in total, including 186 weeks in a row. She won Wimbledon seven times, the Australian Open seven times and the US Open six times. The French Open, on slow clay courts, was her hardest Slam, yet she won it three times.

In January 2017 Serena won the Australian Open, her 23rd Grand Slam singles title, without losing a set. A few months later she announced she had been about eight weeks pregnant during the tournament. Her daughter, Olympia, was born in September 2017.

The birth was difficult and she had serious health problems afterwards. She later spoke out about how Black women in the USA face higher risks during childbirth, and pushed for better care.

Serena often spoke up about equal pay and fair treatment for women athletes. She faced racist abuse at times during her career, and she talked about it openly. In 2001, after a crowd booed her and her family at Indian Wells, she stayed away from that tournament for 14 years.

She also had controversies of her own, such as an angry argument with an umpire in the 2018 US Open final, for which she was fined. She stopped playing after the 2022 US Open and now runs an investment company. Her last match was watched by millions.

text: Sneakers are shoes with soft rubber soles and cloth or leather tops. They became possible in the 1800s, when a way was found to make rubber tough and springy. At first they were simple canvas shoes for sports and games on the beach.

Over the 1900s, athletes made them famous. Runners, [[@tennis|tennis]] players and basketball stars wore them, and companies paid sports heroes to advertise them. By the 1980s, sneakers were fashion as well as sportswear, and today billions of pairs are sold every year. In India, the same shoes are often called "sports shoes" or "PT shoes".

st.reveal: Goodyear found that heating rubber with sulphur made it strong, springy and stable in hot and cold weather. The process is called vulcanisation, after Vulcan, the Roman god of fire.

myth: More expensive sneakers always make you run faster.
A good fit and comfort matter most for everyday running. Some very advanced racing shoes do help top runners a little, but for most children an ordinary, well-fitting pair works just as well.

sec.t:
Natural rubber comes from the sap of rubber trees. On its own, it gets soft and sticky in heat and stiff and cracked in cold. In the USA, the inventor Charles Goodyear spent years trying to fix this, often in debt.

Around 1839, he found that heating rubber with sulphur made it stay strong and springy. He patented the method, called vulcanisation, in 1844. Now rubber could be glued to cloth to make soles that gripped the ground. That grip comes from [[@friction|friction]], the force that resists sliding.

In the small German town of Herzogenaurach, the brothers Adolf and Rudolf Dassler made sports shoes together in the 1920s. At the 1936 Berlin Olympics, the American sprinter Jesse Owens wore their shoes while winning four gold medals.

After the Second World War, the brothers quarrelled. In 1948 they split the company. Adolf, called Adi, founded Adidas, and Rudolf founded Puma. The rivalry divided their town for decades, with factories on opposite sides of the river.

In 1964, an American runner named Phil Knight and his coach began selling running shoes. Their company later became Nike. In 1985, Nike released the Air Jordan, named after the basketball player [[@michael-jordan|Michael Jordan]]. It became one of the best-selling sports shoes ever.

At the same time, [[@hip-hop|hip-hop]] musicians in New York wore sneakers on stage, and people began collecting rare designs. Some collectors keep shoes in their boxes and never wear them. A few rare pairs have sold for huge sums at auction.

In India, the Czech shoe company Bata set up a factory town called Batanagar near [[@kolkata|Kolkata]] in the 1930s. Its white canvas shoes became standard school PT shoes for generations of Indian children.

Today India is one of the world's biggest makers of footwear. Sneakers are worn to school, to the office and to weddings. Most soles are now made from synthetic rubber and foams, materials made from oil, as [[@plastic-made|how plastic is made]] explains. Some companies are trying soles made from recycled plastic and plants, so old shoes don't end up buried in landfills.

text: Superheroes wear capes mostly because of how comics began. The first big comic superhero, Superman, appeared in 1938 with a red cape, blue tights and boots. His creators borrowed from the costumes of circus strongmen, acrobats and stage heroes of the time, who wore tights, belts and sometimes cloaks.

Capes also solved a drawing problem. A comic is a set of still pictures. A cape flowing behind a hero shows speed and wind in a single frame. Because Superman was such a hit, many heroes who followed copied the look.

st.reveal: The early Superman could "leap tall buildings in a single bound", run faster than a train and lift a car. Flying came a few years later, first in cartoons and then in the comics.

sec.t:
Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster were teenagers in Cleveland, Ohio, when they dreamed up Superman in the early 1930s. Publishers turned them down for years. Finally, Superman appeared on the cover of *Action Comics* #1 in June 1938, lifting a car above his head.

The comic sold so well that every publisher wanted its own hero. Batman arrived in 1939, with a dark cape shaped like bat wings. Captain Marvel, Wonder Woman and Captain America soon followed, during the years of the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]].

In a comic, the artist has only still pictures. A flapping cape makes a jump look higher and a punch look faster. Artists draw it streaming behind a running hero or wrapped around one standing in shadow.

Capes are not for everyone, though. Spider-Man, created in 1962, never had one. Neither do many later heroes, who wear armour, masks or plain suits instead. In a 2004 [[@pixar|Pixar]] film about a family of superheroes, a fierce little costume designer famously refuses to make capes. She lists heroes whose capes got caught in [[@plane-jet|jet engines]] and lifts, and the joke has followed capes ever since.

The idea of a superhero is much older than capes. Ancient stories are full of heroes with powers. The Greek hero Hercules had enormous strength, as [[@greek-myths|Greek myths]] tell. In the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]], Hanuman leaps across the sea to Lanka and can change his size at will.

Many comic book writers have said they borrowed from these old stories. Thor, a Marvel hero, comes directly from Norse [[mythology|mythology]]. Wonder Woman's backstory draws on Greek myths about the Amazons.

India has its own caped and uncaped heroes. On TV, *Shaktimaan* (1997) wore a red and gold costume and became a favourite with Indian children. The film *Krrish* (2006) gave [[@bollywood|Bollywood]] a masked superhero. Comics such as [[@myths-indian-creatures|Nagraj]] and Super Commando Dhruva created heroes rooted in Indian settings, as [[@comics-india|India's comics]] describes.

Superhero films are now among the biggest earners in cinemas worldwide. Some heroes still wear capes, some wear armour and some wear hoodies, but the old idea remains: an ordinary-looking person hiding extraordinary powers.

text: Your body is made of trillions of cells. Every day, tiny bits of damage build up inside them. Copying mistakes creep into their [[@dna|DNA]], [[protein|proteins]] get bent out of shape, and waste piles up. Cells can repair much of this damage, but not all of it.

Over many years, the unrepaired damage adds up. Some cells stop dividing, some die, and others stop working well. Skin gets thinner and wrinkles, bones weaken, eyes and ears become less sharp, and the body heals more slowly. That slow wearing-down is ageing.
Why bodies don't simply repair everything for ever is a deeper puzzle. Scientists are still arguing about it.

st.prompt: In the past, average life expectancy was often 30 or 40 years. What was the main reason?

options.t: Many babies and young children died, which pulled the average down
Most adults died around their 30th birthday

st.reveal: An average can mislead. When many children died from infections, the average age of death was low, even though plenty of adults lived into their 60s and 70s. Vaccines, clean water and better food saved children's lives and raised the average.

sec.t:
In 1961, the American scientist Leonard Hayflick noticed something about human [[@body-cells|cells]] grown in a dish. They divided about 40 to 60 times, then stopped. This became known as the Hayflick limit.

Part of the reason lies at the tips of your [[chromosome|chromosomes]], the packages that hold your DNA. These tips, called telomeres, work a bit like the plastic caps on shoelaces. Each time a cell divides, its telomeres get a little shorter. When they get too short, the cell stops dividing. Cells that stop but don't die can also send out signals that cause swelling and damage nearby.

From evolution's point of view, what matters most is surviving long enough to have children and raise them. In the wild, most animals are killed by [[predator|predators]], disease, accidents or hunger long before they grow old. So there was little pressure for bodies to keep themselves perfect into old age.

Some scientists think [[gene|genes]] that help us grow strong when young may cause harm later in life. Others think the body simply puts its energy into growing and having children rather than into perfect repair. Most think both ideas are partly true.

People today live much longer on average than their great-grandparents did. In India around 1950, average life expectancy at birth was only about 35 to 40 years. Today it is about 70. In the USA it is in the high 70s.

The biggest reason is that far fewer children die young, thanks to [[@vaccines|vaccines]], clean water, better food and medicines like [[@antibiotics|antibiotics]]. This has changed the shape of the [[@population|population]]: many countries now have more older people than ever before.

Some things clearly help people stay healthier as they age: being active, eating well, sleeping enough, not smoking and staying connected with friends and family. These don't stop ageing, but they can delay many of the problems that come with it.

Scientists are testing whether drugs or special diets can slow ageing itself. In worms, flies and mice, some have added years, or the equivalent, to lifespans. Whether the same works in people isn't known yet. For now, the oldest humans on record have lived to just over 120, and nobody has beaten Jeanne Calment.

sec.t:
मेलानिन उन कोशिकाओं में बनता है जिन्हें मेलानोसाइट कहते हैं। ये त्वचा की बाहरी परत की तली में बैठी होती हैं। जब सूरज की [[ultraviolet|पराबैंगनी]] रोशनी इन तक पहुँचती है, तो ये त्वचा की रक्षा के लिए ज़्यादा मेलानिन बनाती हैं। धूप में त्वचा इसी तरह साँवली पड़ती है, आम तौर पर कुछ दिनों में।

झाइयों वाले लोगों में मेलानोसाइट एक-सा जवाब नहीं देते। कुछ हिस्से पूरे जोश में आकर खूब रंग बनाने लगते हैं, जबकि उनके बीच की त्वचा हल्की बनी रहती है। नतीजा होता है बिखरे हुए बिंदुओं का एक छिड़काव। झाइयाँ आम तौर पर बचपन की शुरुआत में पहली बार दिखती हैं, और उम्र के साथ अक्सर कम और फीकी हो जाती हैं।

तुम्हें झाइयाँ होंगी या नहीं, यह बहुत हद तक तुम्हारे [[@genes-family|जीन]] पर टिका है। MC1R नाम का एक जीन खास तौर पर अहम है। इसके कुछ रूप शरीर से लाल रंगत वाला मेलानिन ज़्यादा और गहरे रंग वाला कम बनवाते हैं। यही रूप लाल बालों से और ऐसी त्वचा से भी जुड़े हैं जो धूप में जल्दी जल जाती है।

लोग लंबे समय से इन निशानों को मतलब देते आए हैं। 18वीं सदी के यूरोप में फ़ैशन के शौकीन मर्द और औरतें चेहरे पर कपड़े के छोटे काले टुकड़े चिपकाते थे, ताकि वे सौंदर्य-बिंदु जैसे दिखें। भारत के बहुत-से परिवारों में बच्चे के गाल पर या कान के पीछे काजल का एक छोटा काला टीका लगाया जाता है। माना जाता है कि यह बुरी नज़र से बचाता है। चेहरे के तिल का नाम ही छोटे, काले तिल के बीज पर पड़ा है। भारत और चीन, दोनों की चेहरा पढ़ने वाली पुरानी किताबों में दावा किया गया कि तिल की जगह से किसी की किस्मत बताई जा सकती है, हालाँकि इसका कोई वैज्ञानिक सबूत नहीं है।

लगभग सारी झाइयाँ और तिल बेकसूर होते हैं। बहुत ही कम मामलों में कोई तिल त्वचा के एक तरह के कैंसर में बदल सकता है, जिसे मेलानोमा कहते हैं। यह बच्चों के मुकाबले बड़ों में कहीं ज़्यादा होता है, और उन गोरी त्वचा वाले लोगों में जिन्होंने खूब धूप झेली हो।

डॉक्टर सलाह देते हैं कि तिलों में बदलाव पर ABCDE के सहारे नज़र रखो। A यानी बेढंगापन, जब दोनों आधे हिस्से अलग-अलग दिखें। B यानी किनारा, जो कटा-फटा या धुँधला हो। C यानी रंग, जब कई रंग हों या रंग बदल जाए। D यानी चौड़ाई, जो लगभग 6 मिलीमीटर, यानी एक पेंसिल की मोटाई से ज़्यादा हो। E यानी बदलाव, यानी आकार, शक्ल या छूने के एहसास में कोई भी फ़र्क।

अगर किसी तिल में खुजली हो, खून निकले या वह बदल जाए, तो किसी भरोसेमंद बड़े को बताओ, ताकि डॉक्टर उसे देख सकें। धूप वाले दिनों में टोपी पहनना, छाँव ढूँढना और [[@sunburn-sunscreen|सनस्क्रीन]] लगाना त्वचा को, झाइयों समेत, सेहतमंद रखने के आसान तरीके हैं।

text: हँसी इंसानों के बात करने के सबसे पुराने तरीकों में से एक है। शिशु बोलना सीखने से पहले ही हँसने लगते हैं। जो बच्चे जन्म से देख या सुन नहीं सकते, वे भी हँसते हैं। यानी किसी को भी नकल करके हँसना सीखना नहीं पड़ता।

वैज्ञानिक मानते हैं कि हँसी खेल से निकली। जब वानरों के बच्चे कुश्ती लड़ते और एक-दूसरे के पीछे भागते हैं, तो वे हाँफती, फुसफुसाती-सी आवाज़ निकालते हैं, जो कहती है, "यह बस खेल है, मैं सच में हमला नहीं कर रहा।" लाखों सालों में खेल की यह हाँफ शायद [[evolve|विकसित]] होकर इंसानी हँसी की "हा-हा-हा" बन गई। आज हम ज़्यादातर अपनापन दिखाने और दूसरों के साथ कोई एहसास बाँटने के लिए हँसते हैं। चुटकुले इसका बस एक छोटा हिस्सा हैं।

अमेरिकी वैज्ञानिक रॉबर्ट प्रोवाइन ने हँसी को समझने में कई साल लगाए। वे और उनके छात्र शॉपिंग सेंटरों और कॉलेज कैंपसों में बैठकर चुपचाप नोट करते कि हँसने से ठीक पहले लोगों ने क्या कहा। उन्होंने हँसी के एक हज़ार से ज़्यादा पल दर्ज किए।

2009 में मरीना डाविला-रॉस की अगुवाई में एक टीम ने ओरंगउटान, गोरिल्ला, चिंपैंज़ी और बोनोबो के बच्चों की वे आवाज़ें रिकॉर्ड कीं जो वे गुदगुदी होने पर निकालते हैं। फिर उन्होंने इनकी तुलना इंसानी शिशुओं से की। जो [[species|प्रजाति]] इंसानों से जितनी करीबी रिश्तेदार थी, उसकी गुदगुदी वाली हँसी हमारी हँसी से उतनी ही ज़्यादा मिलती थी।

वानरों की हँसी फुसफुसाती-सी होती है और हर साँस के साथ अंदर-बाहर चलती है। इंसान ज़्यादातर साँस छोड़ते हुए, छोटे-छोटे झटकों में हँसते हैं, जिससे हम "हा-हा-हा" की लड़ी बना पाते हैं। [[@tickles|गुदगुदी]] होने पर चूहे भी चीं-चीं करते हैं, पर इतनी ऊँची [[pitch|पिच]] पर कि हम सुन नहीं पाते।

हँसते समय [[diaphragm|डायाफ़्राम]] और छाती की [[@muscles|माँसपेशियाँ]] तेज़, नियमित झटकों में सिकुड़ती हैं। प्रोवाइन ने हँसी के सुरों को मापा तो पाया कि वे एक सेकंड में लगभग पाँच बार आते हैं, और हर "हा" बहुत छोटा होता है। धीरे-धीरे हँसकर देखो, हर दो सेकंड में एक "हा", तो फ़ौरन अजीब लगेगा। लोग असली हँसी और दिखावटी, औपचारिक हँसी में फ़र्क भी काफ़ी अच्छे से पहचान लेते हैं।

[[@yawns|जम्हाई]] की तरह हँसी भी छूत की तरह लगती है। किसी को हँसते सुनकर तुम्हारे हँसने की संभावना बढ़ जाती है। इसीलिए पुराने टीवी कॉमेडी शो अपने कार्यक्रमों में रिकॉर्ड की हुई हँसी जोड़ देते थे।

कभी-कभी यह बहुत दूर तक फैल जाती है। 1962 में, जो इलाका आज तंज़ानिया है, वहाँ लड़कियों के एक बोर्डिंग स्कूल में कुछ छात्राएँ हँसने लगीं और रुक ही नहीं पाईं। कई महीनों में यह दूसरी छात्राओं और आस-पास के गाँवों तक फैल गई, और कुछ स्कूल थोड़े समय के लिए बंद करने पड़े। किसी को गंभीर नुकसान नहीं हुआ। डॉक्टर मानते हैं कि इसमें तनाव और हँसी के छूत वाले स्वभाव, दोनों का हाथ था।

1995 में डॉ. मदन कटारिया ने [[@mumbai|मुंबई]] के एक पार्क में लाफ़्टर क्लब शुरू किया। लोग सुबह इकट्ठा होते और बिना किसी चुटकुले के, जान-बूझकर साथ मिलकर हँसते। नकली हँसी जल्द ही असली बन जाती, क्योंकि हँसी इतनी छूत वाली है। तब से लाफ़्टर योग क्लब कई देशों में फैल चुके हैं।

क्या हँसने से सेहत बेहतर होती है? लगता है कि इससे थोड़ी देर के लिए तनाव घटता है और लोग एक-दूसरे के करीब महसूस करते हैं। कुछ छोटी जाँचें दूसरे फ़ायदे भी बताती हैं। पर बीमारी ठीक कर देने जैसे बड़े दावों का कोई ठोस सबूत नहीं है। फिर भी, [[@akbar-birbal|अकबर-बीरबल]] का कोई किस्सा या कोई कार्टून देखकर दोस्तों के साथ ठहाका लगाना दुनिया की सबसे सस्ती खुशियों में से एक है। तुम्हारा [[@brain-works|दिमाग]] इसका इनाम ऐसे रसायन छोड़कर देता है जिनसे मन ख़ुश हो जाता है।

text: Dirty water can carry three kinds of trouble: bits of dirt you can see, germs you can't, and [[dissolve|dissolved]] chemicals such as salt, arsenic or lead. Different technologies tackle different problems, so treatment plants and home purifiers often use several steps one after another.

Filters strain out dirt. Boiling, chlorine and [[ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light kill germs. Reverse osmosis forces water through a sheet with holes so tiny that salts and most chemicals stay behind. Used well, these tools turn river water, [[@groundwater|groundwater]] and even sea water into water that is safe to drink.

st.prompt: Reverse osmosis purifiers push water through a very fine sheet called a membrane. What gets left behind?

options.t: Salts, germs and most other dissolved things, plus some wasted water
Nothing, it only makes water colder

st.reveal: The membrane's holes are so tiny that only water molecules squeeze through easily. Salts and germs stay behind and are flushed away with some of the water, which is why many RO purifiers waste a litre or more for every litre they clean.

Pour muddy water through and compare it with the muddy water you started with. It looks cleaner, but don't drink it, because a simple filter can't remove germs.
myth: If water looks clear, it is safe to drink.

The germs that cause diseases like cholera and typhoid are far too small to see, and so are chemicals like arsenic or lead. Clear water can still make you ill. Only proper treatment or testing tells you it is safe.

sec.h: Step by step at the treatment plant
sec.t:
A big city's water plant works like a series of sieves and shields. First, chemicals are added that make tiny dirt particles clump together. The clumps sink to the bottom of big tanks. Next, the water trickles through deep beds of sand and gravel, which catch what is left.

Finally, the water is disinfected, usually with chlorine. A small amount stays in the water as it travels through pipes, so germs can't grow on the way to your tap. Jersey City in the United States became the first American city to chlorinate its supply all the time, in 1908, and deaths from typhoid fell sharply wherever chlorine was used.

In many Indian homes, a purifier sits on the kitchen wall. Some use ultraviolet (UV) light, which damages the [[gene|genes]] of germs so they can't multiply. Others use reverse osmosis, or RO, which also removes dissolved salts. RO is useful where groundwater is salty, but it throws away a lot of water and strips out helpful minerals too. Experts say it isn't needed where tap water is already low in salts. A good [[@water-purify|water purifier]] is chosen to match the water you actually have.

Not every solution needs electricity. Clay pot filters, fired with sawdust mixed into the clay, leave tiny holes that trap germs. In the SODIS method, people fill clear plastic bottles and leave them in strong sun for about six hours. Ultraviolet rays and heat together kill most germs.

Boiling remains one of the surest methods, which is why doctors advise it during floods. Powdered seeds of the moringa tree, the drumstick tree common in Indian gardens, can make mud clump and sink. Small household filters of ceramic or cloth now cost very little in many countries.

Coastal cities short of rain are turning to desalination, removing salt from sea water. [[@chennai|Chennai]] opened its first large plant in 2010 and has added more since. In California, a plant near San Diego produces around 190 million litres a day. Desalination uses a lot of energy and pumps very salty water back into the sea, so engineers are working to make it cleaner and cheaper.

Technology is only part of the story. In 2014, the city of Flint in Michigan switched its water supply, and old pipes leaked lead into homes. Good [[@public-health|public health]] also needs well-kept pipes, regular testing, and officials who act when something goes wrong.

text: Bhagat Singh was a young revolutionary who fought British rule in India in the 1920s. He believed that non-violent protest alone would not free India, and he joined a group that used armed action.

He is best known for two acts. In 1928 he and his comrades shot a British police officer in Lahore to avenge the death of the leader Lala Lajpat Rai. In 1929 he threw harmless bombs into the Central Legislative Assembly in Delhi and let himself be arrested. In jail he led a long hunger strike and wrote essays that are still read today. He was hanged in Lahore in 1931, aged only 23. For many Indians, he became a symbol of courage and sacrifice in the [[@freedom-struggle|freedom struggle]].

st.prompt: Why did Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt not run away after throwing bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly?

options.t: They wanted to be arrested so they could speak out at their trial
The doors were locked behind them
They were injured by the bombs

st.reveal: The bombs were made to make noise and smoke, not to kill, and were thrown away from people. The two young men shouted slogans, threw leaflets and waited. They planned to use their trial to tell the whole country why they had acted.

sec.t:
Bhagat Singh was born in 1907 in Banga, a village in [[@punjab|Punjab]] that is now in Pakistan. His father and uncles were part of the freedom movement, and his uncle Ajit Singh had been exiled by the British.

In April 1919, when he was eleven, British troops killed hundreds of unarmed people at [[@jallianwala|Jallianwala Bagh]] in Amritsar. Bhagat Singh is said to have visited the site afterwards, and the massacre affected him deeply. As a teenager, he left college to join the movement.

sec.h: Bombs that were meant not to kill
sec.t:
On 8 April 1929, Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt entered the Central Legislative Assembly in Delhi, the building that later became India's [[@parliament-india|Parliament]] House. They threw two small bombs into empty spaces between the benches. No one was killed.

They shouted "Inquilab Zindabad!", "Long live revolution!", and showered leaflets. One leaflet said that it takes a loud voice to make the deaf hear. Then they stood and waited for the police.

During his trial, Bhagat Singh was linked to the Saunders killing too. In prison, he and other inmates began a hunger strike to demand better treatment for political prisoners, such as books, newspapers and decent food. His comrade Jatin Das died after 63 days without food. Bhagat Singh kept going for about 116 days.

He read constantly, borrowing books on history, politics and [[philosophy|philosophy]]. His prison notebook is full of quotes from writers around the world. He wrote essays explaining his ideas, including "Why I Am an Atheist".

Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were sentenced to death. Many Indians begged for mercy, and [[@gandhi|Gandhi]] raised their case with the Viceroy. Whether Gandhi could have done more is still argued about.

On 23 March 1931, the three were hanged in Lahore jail, a day earlier than planned. Their bodies were secretly cremated near Hussainiwala on the Sutlej river. A memorial now stands there, close to the border with [[@pakistan-history|Pakistan]], and 23 March is marked as Martyrs' Day in their memory.

text: Jyotirao Phule, often called Mahatma Phule or Jyotiba, was a social reformer, writer and thinker from Pune in the 1800s. He fought against [[@caste-history|caste]] discrimination, the unfair treatment of people based on the community they were born into. He also worked for the education of girls and of children who had been denied schooling.

With his wife [[@savitribai-phule|Savitribai Phule]], he opened a school for girls in 1848. In 1873 he founded a society called the Satyashodhak Samaj, or Truth-Seekers' Society, to work for equal rights.

st.prompt: Phule's book Gulamgiri was dedicated to whom?

options.t: Americans who fought to end slavery
The students of his first school

st.reveal: Phule saw a link between slavery in America and caste discrimination in India. He dedicated Gulamgiri to the good people of the United States who had worked to free enslaved people.

d.try: With a family member, find out who the important reformers were in your own state or city, a hundred or more years ago. Choose one and write five sentences about what they changed. Share it with your class or a friend.
myth: Mahatma Gandhi was the first Indian to be called "Mahatma".
Jyotirao Phule was given the title Mahatma at a public meeting in Bombay in 1888, when Gandhi was still a teenager. The title means "great soul" and has been given to several people.

sec.t:
Jyotirao was born in 1827 in a family of gardeners and flower sellers. The family name Phule comes from the Marathi word for flowers. His mother died when he was a baby, and his father, Govindrao, brought him up.

He went to a Scottish mission school in [[@pune|Pune]], where he did well and read widely. One book that moved him was *Rights of Man* by Thomas Paine, an English-American writer who argued that all people are born with equal rights. Jyotirao began to ask why Indian society treated people so unequally.

A story he told later describes a moment in 1848. He joined a friend's wedding procession, but some guests insulted him because of his caste and told him to leave. He was hurt and angry, and he decided to spend his life fighting such unfairness.

He believed education was the key. That same year, he and Savitribai began teaching girls. Soon they opened schools for children from communities that had been kept out of classrooms. Many people opposed them, and at one point they had to leave his father's home.

The couple also took on problems few others would touch. Young widows at the time were often shunned, and some were driven to despair. In 1863 the Phules opened a home where such women could give birth in safety. Jyotirao also spoke up for widows' right to remarry, which many people then considered shameful.

{{story:caste-history}}

In 1873 Phule published *Gulamgiri*, meaning Slavery. It argued that the caste system kept millions of Indians in a kind of bondage. Phule had followed news of the [[@slavery-freedom|American fight against slavery]], which had ended with the Civil War only eight years earlier.

He dedicated the book to the good people of the United States, praising those who had worked to free enslaved people. It was an unusual link to draw at the time, between struggles on opposite sides of the world.

The Satyashodhak Samaj, founded the same year, welcomed people of all castes and religions. It encouraged simple weddings without expensive priests and pushed for schooling for all. Its members held meetings in villages and wrote in plain Marathi so farmers could follow their ideas. Its members spread across Maharashtra.

Phule also wrote about [[@jobs-farmer|farmers]], who were often deep in debt. His book *Shetkaryacha Asud*, or The Cultivator's Whipcord, described how hard their lives were. He once opened the water tank at his house to people who had been refused water from public wells.

In 1888, at a public meeting in Bombay, he was given the title Mahatma, meaning "great soul". He died in Pune on 28 November 1890. After his death, Savitribai carried on leading the Satyashodhak Samaj.

His ideas shaped later leaders. [[@ambedkar|B.R. Ambedkar]], who helped write India's Constitution, named Phule as one of his three great teachers, along with the Buddha and the poet-saint Kabir. Today schools, universities, roads and markets across Maharashtra carry his name, including Mahatma Phule Mandai, a famous old market in Pune. His birthday, 11 April, is marked across India.

text: In 1498 the Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa and landed near Kozhikode (Calicut) in Kerala. Portugal wanted a sea route to buy [[@spices|spices]] directly, without going through the Arab and Venetian traders who controlled the old routes. Within a few years, Portuguese warships were trying to control trade along India's west coast.

They captured Goa in 1510 and built forts and trading posts from Gujarat to Sri Lanka. They brought Catholic missionaries, new crops and new words. Their rule was often harsh, especially towards people of other faiths. Goa stayed Portuguese for over 450 years, and Daman and Diu for about 400, until India took them in 1961.

myth: The British were the first Europeans to rule part of India.
The Portuguese arrived first, in 1498, and controlled Goa from 1510, more than 100 years before the English East India Company set up its first factory. They also left last, in 1961.

sec.t:
For centuries, Indian pepper, cinnamon and cloves reached Europe through long chains of traders across the Arabian Sea, Egypt and the Mediterranean. Each middleman added to the price. Portugal, a small country on the edge of Europe, decided to go around them.

Vasco da Gama's four ships left Lisbon in 1497. With help from a local pilot who knew the [[monsoon|monsoon]] winds, they crossed from East Africa to India in under four weeks. The ruler of Calicut, called the Zamorin, was not impressed by the cheap gifts da Gama offered. But the spices da Gama carried home were worth many times the cost of the voyage.

Portuguese rule brought Catholic missionaries. Francis Xavier, a Spanish priest who worked in Goa and along the south Indian coast in the 1540s, is buried in the Basilica of Bom Jesus in Old Goa. The churches and convents of Old Goa are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

There was also a darker side. From 1560, the Goa Inquisition, a church court, persecuted Hindus, Muslims, Jews and new converts accused of keeping old practices. Many temples were destroyed. Many Goan families moved away to keep their faith. The Inquisition was finally ended in 1812.

Portuguese ships carried plants from the Americas to India. Chillies, which now flavour almost every Indian kitchen, arrived this way in the 1500s. So did [[@cashew|cashews]], papayas, pineapples, guavas and potatoes. The cashew trees planted to hold Goa's soil now support a whole industry, including the local drink feni.

The Portuguese also taught bakers in Goa to make leavened bread. The soft bread roll called pav takes its name from the Portuguese *pão*. Mumbai's vada pav and pav bhaji owe their bread to that history. Portuguese-style dishes like vindaloo grew from Portuguese recipes mixed with Goan spices.

Portuguese words slipped into Hindi, Marathi, Konkani, Bengali and other languages: chabi for key, almari for cupboard, balti for bucket, girja for church and mistri for a skilled worker. Many Goan, Mangalorean and Kerala Christian families still carry Portuguese surnames such as D'Souza, Fernandes and Pereira.

As other European powers grew, Portugal lost most of its Indian [[territory|territories]]. By the 1900s it held only Goa, Daman, Diu and Dadra and Nagar Haveli. After independence, India asked Portugal to leave, but it refused. In December 1961, Indian troops entered Goa, and Portuguese rule ended within two days, a story told in [[@goa-liberation|Goa's liberation]]. Today [[@goa|Goa]] is India's smallest state by area, and its whitewashed churches, red-tiled houses and Konkani songs still carry traces of those 450 years.

text: The Pony Express was a mail service that used relays of riders on fast horses to carry letters across the western United States. It ran from April 1860 to October 1861, between St Joseph, Missouri, and Sacramento, California, about 3,100 km (1,900 miles).

Before it began, mail from the East Coast could take weeks or months to reach California by ship or stagecoach. The Pony Express cut that to about 10 days. It ended almost as soon as the first [[telegraph|telegraph]] line crossed the continent, which could send a message in minutes.

st.prompt: How often did a Pony Express rider usually swap to a fresh horse?

options.t: Never, each rider kept one horse all the way

st.reveal: Horses tire quickly at a gallop, so small relay stations were built about every 15 to 25 km. A rider jumped onto a fresh horse in a couple of minutes and kept going. After about 120 km or more, a new rider took over.

myth: The Pony Express ran for many years and was the main way Americans sent mail west.
It ran for only about 18 months. Most mail still went by slower stagecoach or ship. The Pony Express carried urgent letters and news for people who could afford its high prices.
