sec.t:
Pony Express riders were usually young and light, often teenagers, because every kilogram slowed the horse. Each rode about 120 km or more on a shift, swapping horses roughly every 15 to 25 km at small stations. A swap took only a couple of minutes.

The mail travelled in a leather cover called a mochila, with locked pockets for letters, which fitted over the saddle. A rider could whip it off one horse and throw it onto the next in seconds. Riders galloped through blizzards, deserts and darkness, day and night. A full run from Missouri to California needed dozens of riders and hundreds of horse changes.

The fastest Pony Express run ever carried President [[@abraham-lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]]'s first inaugural address, from March 1861. Riders took it from the end of the telegraph line in Nebraska to the western end of the line in Nevada in about 7 days and 17 hours.

The speech mattered. Southern states were leaving the Union, and Californians were anxious to know how Lincoln would respond. Within weeks, the [[@us-civil-war|Civil War]] began.

Sending a letter by Pony Express was costly. At first, it cost $5 for half an ounce, about 14 g, which was a lot of money then, perhaps a week's wages for many workers. Prices later dropped, but the service never made a profit.

On 24 October 1861, the transcontinental [[@telegraph|telegraph]] was completed. Messages that took riders 10 days could now be tapped out in Morse code in minutes. Two days later, the Pony Express announced it would close. Its owners lost a fortune.

Many stories about the Pony Express grew in the telling. Buffalo Bill Cody, the famous showman, claimed he rode for it as a boy, but historians aren't sure. Wild West shows and films later made the riders into heroes facing constant danger.

Real dangers existed, from weather, rivers and accidents. During a war with the Paiute people in Nevada in 1860, some stations were attacked and burned. But records suggest only one load of mail was ever lost.

India had its own relay mail long before the Pony Express. Runners called dak harkaras carried mail in stages, often at a jog, ringing bells to warn off wild animals and robbers. That system, described in the story of the [[@oddity-hindustani-mail|Hindustani mail]], lasted into the 1900s in remote areas, much longer than America's famous horse riders.

text: The Pamban Bridge carries trains across the sea from mainland Tamil Nadu to Rameswaram, a holy island town. It is special twice over. The old bridge, opened in 1914, was India's first sea bridge, and it worked for more than a hundred years in salty, stormy water. The new bridge, opened beside it on 6 April 2025, is India's first vertical-lift sea bridge.

In the middle of the new bridge, a 72-metre section of track can rise straight up between two towers, like a giant lift. That lets ships and fishing boats pass through the channel underneath. When the ships have gone, the span comes down and the trains roll across again.

st.prompt: How does the middle of the new Pamban Bridge let ships through?

options.t: A whole section of track rises straight up, staying flat, like a lift
Two halves swing upwards like a drawbridge
The section slides sideways out of the way

st.reveal: The new bridge has a vertical-lift span. Motors raise the 72-metre section straight up between two towers, keeping it level. The old bridge was different. Its two halves tilted upwards, like the jaws of a crocodile opening.

sec.t:
Rameswaram sits on Pamban Island, in the narrow sea between India and [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]]. It is one of Hinduism's most important [[pilgrimage|pilgrimage]] places, with the Ramanathaswamy Temple at its heart. Before 1914, pilgrims had to cross by boat.

The British built the railway bridge from 1911 to 1914. It was about 2.07 km long and stood on more than 140 piers in the sea. For decades it also linked to a ferry from Dhanushkodi, at the tip of the island, to Sri Lanka. Until a road bridge opened in 1988, the train was the only way to reach the island over land.

In December 1964, a powerful [[@cyclones-india|cyclone]] hit the coast. Huge waves wrecked much of the bridge and destroyed the town of Dhanushkodi. A passenger train on the Dhanushkodi line was swept away, and well over 100 people on board died, though counts vary.

Engineers expected repairs to take months. A young railway engineer, E. Sreedharan, led the team that got trains back on the bridge in just 46 days. He later became famous for building the Konkan Railway and the Delhi Metro.

The new bridge runs right beside the old one. It is about 2.07 km long, with 99 short spans and one long lifting span. The piers go deep into the seabed, and the steel is protected with special coatings meant to resist salt for decades.

The deck sits about 3 metres higher than the old one. When the lift span is fully raised, ships up to about 22 metres tall can pass, roughly the height of a seven-storey building. The bridge was built by Rail Vikas Nigam Limited, a government railway company, at a cost of about ₹500 crore. It was designed for electric trains and for two tracks in future.

For now, the old bridge still stands next to the new one, rusting quietly, its jaws frozen in place. It may be kept as a heritage monument. On a calm day, you can see both from the road bridge: a century of engineering side by side in turquoise water. India's bridges across the sea have grown longer since, from the [[@india-wonder-bandra-sealink|Bandra-Worli Sea Link]] in Mumbai to the 21.8 km Atal Setu, but Pamban was the first to try.

text: Feluda and Professor Shonku are two characters created by the Bengali film-maker and writer Satyajit Ray. Both first appeared in *Sandesh*, the children's magazine his grandfather had started and his father had run.

Feluda is a [[@detective-stories|private detective]] from [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], clever, calm and very observant, who solves mysteries across India and beyond. Professor Shonku is an eccentric scientist and inventor whose adventures are told through entries in his diary. Ray wrote more than thirty stories about each, illustrated many himself, and turned two Feluda stories into [[@childrens-films-india|films]]. They remain among the best-loved books in Bengali, and English translations have found readers across India.

sec.t:
Feluda's full name is Prodosh Chandra Mitter. He first appeared in 1965 in "Feludar Goendagiri", "Feluda's Detective Work". He is a big admirer of [[@sherlock-holmes|Sherlock Holmes]], does yoga, has a sharp memory and is calm in a crisis.

His stories are told by his young cousin, Tapesh, nicknamed Topshe, who follows him everywhere. From 1971, they are joined by Lalmohan Ganguly, a writer of silly thrillers who uses the pen name Jatayu. His car, his mistakes and his nervous courage give the stories much of their humour.

Feluda's cases take him to [[@varanasi|Varanasi]], Darjeeling, Lucknow, Kathmandu and London. Readers learn a lot about history, art and geography along the way. Ray kept the stories free of gore, so that children could enjoy them.

{{story:rajasthan-forts}}

In *Sonar Kella*, a boy in Kolkata claims to remember a past life in a "golden fort" with peacocks and buried jewels. Feluda's team travels to Rajasthan, chased by criminals who want the treasure, to find the fort.

Ray filmed the story in 1974 at Jaisalmer, whose fort of yellow sandstone glows gold in the sun, one of the great [[@rajasthan-forts|Rajasthan forts]]. The film was a huge hit with Bengali audiences, and many began visiting Jaisalmer because of it.

Ray's second Feluda film, *Joi Baba Felunath* (1979), was set in Varanasi.

Trilokeshwar Shonku first appeared in 1961 in "Byomjatrir Diary", "The Diary of a Space Traveller". He lives in Giridih, a small town now in Jharkhand, with his cat, Newton, and his servant, Prahlad.

Shonku's inventions are wonderfully strange. Miracurall is a pill that cures almost any illness. The Annihilin pistol can make an attacker vanish into thin air. He builds a [[@robots|robot]] named Bidhushekhar, who develops a mind of its own. He travels to Mars in his very first story, later to remote corners of the Earth, and meets scientists from around the world.

The stories mix real science with fantasy, and Shonku is honest about failures. Like many real experiments, his inventions sometimes work in ways he never expected.

sec.h: A writer who drew his own world
sec.t:
Ray came from a family of storytellers. His father, Sukumar Ray, wrote famous nonsense verse, and his grandfather, Upendrakishore, wrote children's stories. When Satyajit revived *Sandesh* in 1961, he needed stories to fill it, so he wrote them.

He was already world famous for films like *Pather Panchali* (1955), and in 1992 he received an honorary Oscar for his life's work. Yet many Bengali readers know him first as the man who gave them Feluda. Ray designed the covers of his books, drew the illustrations, and even created typefaces. Few writers have controlled every detail of how their stories looked.

text: Most candy is made by [[dissolve|dissolving]] [[@sugar|sugar]] in water and boiling it. As the syrup boils, water escapes as steam and the syrup gets thicker and hotter. Candy makers stop at a particular temperature depending on what they want to make.

Stop at a lower temperature and you get soft fudge or chewy caramel. Keep going and you get toffee. Go all the way to about 150 °C and almost no water is left, so the syrup cools into hard, glassy candy, like a lollipop. Colours, flavours, milk, butter, nuts or [[@chocolate-world|chocolate]] are added along the way. Boiling sugar is far hotter than boiling water and sticks to skin, so it is a job for experienced adults.

st.prompt: What makes a lollipop hard and glassy, while fudge is soft and crumbly?

options.t: The lollipop syrup was boiled hotter, leaving almost no water
Fudge is made from a different kind of sugar

st.reveal: The hotter sugar syrup gets, the more water boils away. At about 150 °C almost no water is left, and the sugar cools into a hard glass. Fudge is cooked to a lower temperature and stirred, so it forms tiny crystals and stays soft.

Careful studies, in which neither parents nor children knew who had eaten sugar, found no real difference in behaviour. Parents who believed their child had eaten sugar were more likely to rate the child as hyper. Sugar is still bad for teeth.

sec.t:
Before cheap thermometers, cooks tested syrup by feel and by eye. Indian sweet-makers still do. They dip a finger and thumb in a little cooled syrup, called chashni, and pull them apart. If one sticky thread forms, it is ek taar, one-string syrup. Two threads, do taar, mean a thicker syrup. Each sweet needs its own stage, and a minute too long on the fire can turn a soft [[@food-laddoo|laddoo]] into a rock.

Candy makers in Europe and America used a similar trick. They dropped a little syrup into cold water and checked whether it formed a soft ball, a firm ball or snapped like glass. Recipe books still use these names today: soft ball for fudge, hard crack for brittle and lollipops.

sec.h: A word that came from India
sec.t:
People in India were among the first to turn sugarcane juice into solid crystals, more than 1,500 years ago. The [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] word for a piece of sugar was *khanda*. It passed into Persian and then Arabic as *qand*, and came into English as "candy". Even the word "sugar" can be traced back to the Sanskrit *sharkara*.

For a long time sugar was rare and costly in Europe, and sweets were a luxury for the rich. Only in the 1800s, when sugar became cheap and machines could make sweets in huge amounts, did candy become something ordinary children could buy with a coin.

Cotton candy is hard candy spun into threads. A machine heats sugar until it melts, then flings it through tiny holes in a spinning bowl. The streams cool instantly into threads thinner than a hair, which collect like wool around a stick.

The electric machine was patented in the 1890s by a dentist, William Morrison, and a sweet-maker, John C. Wharton. They sold their "fairy floss" at the 1904 World's Fair in St. Louis. In India it is often called buddhi ke baal, an old woman's hair, and is sold at fairs and beaches.

Hard and sticky sweets stay in your mouth a long time, which gives [[bacteria|bacteria]] on your teeth a long feast. That is why dentists worry about them more than about a piece of cake eaten quickly. Brushing and drinking water after sweets help protect [[@sugar-teeth|your teeth]].

text: Cashews came to India from Brazil. Portuguese traders found the cashew tree growing in northeastern Brazil in the 1500s and carried it on their ships to their colonies, including Goa. The tree grew well along India's warm, sandy coasts, and within a few centuries it had spread through Goa, Kerala, Karnataka and beyond.

Today India is one of the world's biggest processors and eaters of cashews. Kollam in Kerala became a famous cashew processing centre. India also [[import|imports]] raw cashew nuts, mainly from Africa, shells and roasts them, and sends them around the world.

st.prompt: Shops sell "raw cashews". Have they really never been heated?

options.t: No, all cashews are heated during processing to remove the shell's harmful oil
Yes, they are picked straight from the tree and packed
Yes, but they are washed in salt water

st.reveal: The cashew shell contains an oil that can burn the skin. So every cashew is roasted or steamed before shelling. "Raw" cashews have simply not been roasted again for flavour.

sec.t:
The cashew tree grows a fleshy, pear-shaped fruit called a cashew apple. It can be red, orange or yellow. The actual nut hangs from its bottom in a hard, kidney-shaped shell. It looks almost like a mistake.

The cashew apple is juicy but soft and spoils quickly, so it's rarely sold far from where it grows. In Goa, it's used to make a strong drink for adults called feni. The nut is what's traded around the world.

In the 1500s, Portuguese ships sailed between Brazil, Africa and India along their [[@trade-routes|sea trade routes]]. They carried many American plants, including chillies, pineapples, [[@guava-papaya|papayas]] and cashews. Cashew trees were probably growing in Goa by the late 1500s.

A common story says the Portuguese planted cashews on India's coast to hold sandy soil in place and [[@cliffs-erosion|stop erosion]]. The trees certainly grew well in poor, sandy soils where few other crops thrived. Over time, local farmers began to value the nuts.

Processing cashews takes a lot of work. The nuts are first roasted or steamed. Then the shells are cracked open one by one, often by hand or with a simple foot-operated cutter. The thin brown skin around each nut is peeled off, and the nuts are sorted by size and colour.

In Kerala, much of this work has long been done by women. The shell oil can damage their hands, so many wear gloves or rub their hands with oil. Workers' health and fair pay have been important issues in the industry. Today some factories use machines for parts of the job.

India started exporting cashews in the early 1900s, and they became an important [[export|export]] for Kerala. In the USA, cashews became a popular snack. Today the biggest grower of raw cashews is Côte d'Ivoire in West Africa, but India remains a major processor.

Cashews go into [[@sweets-india|Indian sweets]] like kaju katli, rich gravies in Mughlai dishes, and Goan cooking. Some people are allergic to them, as with other tree nuts, which can be serious. If someone has a [[@food-allergies|nut allergy]], even a tiny amount can cause trouble.

text: Around the world, hundreds of millions of children eat lunch at school every day. What's on the plate depends on where they live. In India, it might be rice, dal and vegetables. In Japan, it could be fish, miso soup and rice. In France, children may get a starter, a main course, cheese and fruit.

Most countries see school meals as more than food. A good lunch helps children concentrate, grow and stay healthy. In poorer places, a free meal can be the reason a child comes to school at all. The way lunch is served also teaches something about each country: how people share, what they value and what grows nearby.

sec.t:
India runs the biggest school meal programme on Earth. Under a scheme called PM POSHAN, about 11 crore children in government schools got a free hot lunch in 2025. Most meals are cooked fresh in school kitchens or big central kitchens, then served on steel plates.

The idea grew over a century. Madras (now Chennai) served meals in some schools in the 1920s, and Tamil Nadu spread them widely from the 1950s. In 2001, India's Supreme Court ordered every state to give cooked meals in government primary schools. The [[@mid-day-meal|mid-day meal]] is now the main meal of the day for many children. Menus vary: eggs in some states, [[@millets|millets]] in others, and [[@rice|rice]] or rotis depending on the region.

France treats lunch as a proper sit-down meal that can take an hour. Many school canteens serve several small courses, often including a piece of cheese, and children are expected to taste a bit of everything.

Finland has served free school meals to every pupil since 1948. Children help themselves from a buffet, and teachers often eat with them. In Brazil, a law passed in 2009 says at least 30% of the money spent on school food must buy from local family farms. That gives children fresh fruit and gives small farmers a steady customer.

In the USA, the National School Lunch Program began in 1946. Schools served more than 4.8 billion lunches in 2024. Families on low incomes get them free or cheap. A typical tray has sections for a main dish, fruit, vegetables, grain and a carton of milk.

American school lunches have long sparked arguments over what counts as healthy. In 2011, Congress let the tomato paste on pizza count as a vegetable serving, and people joked that pizza had become a vegetable. New rules since then have added more whole grains and cut salt.

[[nutrition|Nutrition]] experts agree on the basics. A good school lunch has a mix of grains, [[protein|protein]], vegetables and fruit, with not too much sugar or salt. These give the [[@food-nutrients|nutrients]] children need for growing bones and busy brains.

Beyond that, every country does it its own way. Korean pupils eat kimchi with almost every lunch. Children in Kenya might get a stew of maize and beans called githeri. A tray in Ohio and a steel plate in Odisha look nothing alike. Both are trying to make sure a hungry child can learn after lunch.

text: Food in India changes with the land, the weather and history. In the wet east and south, where rice grows well, rice is the main grain. In the cooler, drier north and northwest, people eat more wheat breads. In hot, dry areas, millets like bajra and jowar were long the everyday grain.

Coastal regions cook with fish and coconut. Inland, [[@lentils-world|lentils]], vegetables and milk matter more. On top of that, traders and rulers from Persia, Portugal, Britain and beyond brought new ingredients and dishes. That's why a meal in Kolkata can taste nothing like a meal in Chennai or Jaipur.

d.try: Ask three adults from different families what oil or fat they cook with at home, and which grain they eat most. Mark their answers on an outline map of India. See whether you can spot a pattern between where families come from and what they cook with.
myth: All Indian food is "curry", made with curry powder.

The word curry was used by the British for almost any Indian dish with a sauce. Indian cooks traditionally mix different spices for each dish, and a single ready-made curry powder isn't part of most home cooking.

ghee, mustard oil, coconut oil, groundnut oil, sesame oil

sec.t:
The cooking fat changes the taste of a whole cuisine. Kerala cooks with [[@oils-cooking|coconut oil]]. Bengal and Odisha love pungent mustard oil. Gujarat and much of the Deccan cook with groundnut oil, while Tamil Nadu often uses sesame oil, called gingelly or nallennai. In the north, ghee is prized.

Each fat came from what grew nearby. Coconut palms line Kerala's coast, mustard grows across the northern and eastern plains, and groundnuts thrive in Gujarat's soils. A [[@bengali-food|fish curry]] cooked in mustard oil in Kolkata and one cooked in coconut oil in [[@kochi|Kochi]] can taste like two different dishes, even with the same fish.

[[@food-pepper-black-gold|Black pepper]] grows wild in the forests of the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]]. Turmeric, cardamom, ginger and cinnamon have been used in South Asia for thousands of years. Traders from Rome, Arabia and China came to India for them.

Then, in the 1500s, Portuguese traders brought plants from the Americas: [[@chillies|chillies]], tomatoes, potatoes, peanuts and [[@cashew|cashews]]. Within a century or two, chillies had spread so widely that it's now hard to picture Indian food without them.

The [[@mughals|Mughals]], who ruled much of North India from the 1500s, brought Persian and Central Asian cooking. Rich gravies with nuts and cream, kebabs and pulao became famous in Delhi, Lucknow and Hyderabad.

The Portuguese shaped [[@goan-food|Goan food]], with vinegar and bread. Parsis who came from Persia created dishes like dhansak. Chinese families in Kolkata invented [[@chinese-food-india|Indian-Chinese food]], such as chilli chicken and hakka noodles. The British left behind tea time, cutlets and the word "curry".

Religion and custom shape the plate too. Many Jains avoid root vegetables such as onions, potatoes and garlic. Some Hindu communities eat no meat, while others, including many Bengali and Kashmiri families, eat fish or meat regularly. Gujarat and Rajasthan have large vegetarian populations.

Festivals bring their own dishes, from modaks for Ganesh Chaturthi in Maharashtra to pithas in Assam and Odisha. Across India, you could eat a different regional dish every day for a year and still not run out.
